title: Short Stuff: Poutine: Canada's Pride
summary: Short Stuff episode on poutine, Canada's signature dish of French fries, cheese curds, and brown gravy. Josh and Chuck trace its origins to rural Centre-du-Quebec in the 1950s, with competing inventor claims: Fernand La Chance of Cafe Ideal in Warwick (fries with curds, 1957; gravy added 1963) and Jean Paul Roy of Drummondville (Le Roy Jucep, patate sauce, 1958-1964). They discuss the possible etymology ("pudding" or "poutine" as slang for mess), spread to Quebec City (1969) and Montreal (1983), regional variations, the American "disco fries" name, fast-food adoption by Quebec Freetz Frites (1985), Burger King franchisee Jean Louis Roy (1987), McDonald's (1990) and Harvey's (1992), and the 2000s gourmet poutine trend led by Martin Picard's foie gras version, with chef Hugh Acheson criticizing it.
topics: French fries with cheese curds and gravy

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Short Stuff episode, noting they are on their own, and tease poutine as Canada's national dish.

segments.title: Poutine appeal and calories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how much they like poutine, its calorie and fat content, and why it suits cold Quebec winters.

segments.title: Poutine's rural Quebec beginnings
segments.summary: Poutine appeared in 1950s snack bars in rural Quebec and later reached fast food menus and Ontario. The hosts introduce Centre-du-Quebec as the origin area and mention the cheese makers who supply the curds.

segments.title: Fernand La Chance and Cafe Idéal
segments.summary: Fernand La Chance of Cafe Idéal in Warwick says a customer, Eddie Linness, asked him to add curds to fries in 1957. Gravy came later, around 1963. The hosts note the French-language quip and the paper-bag and plate serving history.

segments.title: Jean Paul Roy and patate sauce
segments.summary: Jean Paul Roy of Drummondville says he served fries with a sauce called patate sauce from 1958 and added curds at Le Roy Jucep in 1964, naming the dish fromage patate sauce. He had to source heavy containers from Toronto.

segments.title: Etymology of the word poutine
segments.summary: The hosts discuss theories for the name poutine, including a link to English 'pudding' and to French slang for mess, and note that no origin is agreed on.

segments.title: Spread across Quebec, Canada, and regional variations
segments.summary: Poutine moved to Quebec City in 1969 and Montreal in 1983. Variations include Italian, veggie, Montreal-style smoked meat, and a Korean-style version in Toronto.

segments.title: Disco fries in the United States
segments.summary: By the 1970s poutine reached New York and New Jersey under the name disco fries, using mozzarella rather than curds. The hosts say the curds lose their squeak after a few days.

segments.title: Fast food chains: Freetz Frites and Burger King
segments.summary: Quebec chain Freetz Frites offered poutine in 1985 and was an early national or regional chain to do so. Burger King franchisee Jean Louis Roy began selling it in 1987, and Burger King expanded it to Quebec restaurants.

segments.title: McDonald's, Harvey's, and gourmet poutine
segments.summary: McDonald's added poutine in Quebec in 1990 and later across Canada, and Harvey's followed in 1992. In the 2000s, chefs elevated poutine, with Martin Picard's foie gras version as an early example.

segments.title: Chef Hugh Acheson on gourmet poutine
segments.summary: Chefs added lobster and braised beef to poutine, moving it away from its roots. Chef Hugh Acheson, who grew up in Ottawa with poutine, criticized the upscale versions as comforting garbage food. Chuck notes Acheson's Atlanta and Athens restaurants.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck suggest visiting Quebec or making poutine at home, and Chuck says he may try it at a local Atlanta restaurant. The show closes with the standard iHeartRadio credit.
